newsitem.title: UK: Oral drug still useful despite test stop-sources.
newsitem.headline: Oral drug still useful despite test stop-sources.

text.p: A drug used orally to treat lung cancer since 1983 remains a useful weapon against the disease, industry sources said on Thursday, reacting to a decision by British researchers to stop a study on etoposide tablets.
The researchers said using etoposide tablets alone did not work against small-cell lung cancer, an illness that has frustrated doctors for years because it does not respond to drugs.
Dr David Girling and colleagues at the Medical Research Council were testing etoposide tablets alone versus intravenous etoposide plus other cancer drugs in 339 seriously ill patients.

"Before the planned intake of 450 patients had been completed the trial was stopped on the recommendation of an independent data monitoring committee, because of the inferiority of oral etoposide," they wrote in the Lancet medical journal last week.

They had hoped etoposide would work against the cancer. But at six months, 35 percent of patients given etoposide were alive, compared to 49 percent of controls given intravenous combinations of drugs.

"The reason why were doing the trial is because (etoposide tablets are) being increasingly used, because it's so easy to just take a tablet. People should not just use new ways of using drugs like this unless they've been assessed," Girling said.
Industry sources said the test had not yet been fully evaluated and oral tablets still had their uses where patients were too old or ill to undergo intravenous treatment.
Matti Aapro of the European Institute of Oncology in Milan said the findings reported in the Lancet did not mean the drug should not be used.
"It is too early to dismiss oral etoposide, since data on quality of life have not been presented in full and data on survival are not quite convincing," Aapro wrote in a commentary in Nature.

"Etoposide is active against many tumour types, and its oral form could well be combined with other oral agents, including topotecan, which when given intravenously is an extremely active agent against small-cell cancer."
Etoposide is made by Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. It was first used in the 1970s.
